title: 1 Kings 9:1–9
context: After Solomon finishes the temple and his palace, the LORD appears to him a second time, as at Gibeon (3:5). God answers the dedication prayer of chapter 8: he has made the house holy and set his name there, and his eyes and heart will be there. Then come a promise and a warning. If Solomon walks before God as David did, his throne will be established as promised to David (2 Samuel 7:12–16). If Solomon or his descendants turn to other gods, Israel will be cut off from the land, the house cast from God’s sight, and passersby will ask why. The answer will be that they abandoned the LORD. Both traditions read this as shared ground: God’s promise to David stands, his presence is real, and covenant unfaithfulness brings real judgment, as the exile later shows (2 Kings 25). The broader question of whether God’s people persevere to the end is treated in the site’s existing box at 1 Samuel 12:22, and the Davidic covenant was treated as shared ground at 2 Samuel 7. This passage adds no separate contrast.

verses.text: When Solomon had finished the building of the LORD’s house, the king’s house, and all Solomon’s desire which he was pleased to do,
verses.arminianNotes:
When Solomon has finished building the LORD’s house, his own palace, and all he desired to build, the scene is set for God’s response. The building program is complete.

Arminian readers note that Solomon’s achievements are real and good, yet the narrative immediately turns to God’s word, reminding readers that faithfulness, not accomplishment, is what God will look for in the king.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the completion of the temple fulfills the promise that David’s son would build a house for God’s name (2 Samuel 7:13), and that God now speaks to confirm and frame what he has graciously brought about.

Both traditions see the finished work as a gift that calls for continued faithfulness.

verses.text: The LORD appeared to Solomon the second time, as he had appeared to him at Gibeon.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD appears to Solomon a second time, as he had at Gibeon. The earlier appearance came at the start of his reign (3:5).

Arminian readers note that God renews his personal word to Solomon, showing his ongoing relationship with the king and giving him fresh opportunity to respond in faithfulness at the height of his success.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s second appearance is an act of covenant grace, as God takes the initiative to speak again, and that the later statement that Solomon turned away despite two appearances (11:9) shows the seriousness of what follows.

Both traditions see this appearance as a gracious privilege that heightens Solomon’s responsibility.

verses.text: The LORD said to him, “I have heard your prayer and your supplication that you have made before me. I have made this house holy, which you have built, to put my name there forever; and my eyes and my heart shall be there perpetually.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says he has heard Solomon’s prayer, has made the house holy to put his name there forever, and that his eyes and heart will be there perpetually. God answers the dedication prayer.

Arminian readers note that God’s promise to be present answers a prayer freely offered, showing that God responds to the prayers of his people and delights to dwell among them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God himself makes the house holy; its holiness comes from his choice and presence, not from the builders’ work, and his attention to it rests on his own name and purpose.

Both traditions affirm the reality of God’s promised presence, while also hearing the warning in verse 7 that the house could be cast away.

verses.text: As for you, if you will walk before me as David your father walked, in integrity of heart and in uprightness, to do according to all that I have commanded you, and will keep my statutes and my ordinances,
verses.arminianNotes:
God tells Solomon that if he walks before him as David did, in integrity and uprightness, keeping his commands, statutes and ordinances, a promise will follow. The standard is David’s walk.

Arminian readers note that the conditional language calls Solomon to genuine, ongoing faithfulness, and that the king’s choices really matter for how the promise is experienced in his reign and that of his descendants.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s walk is held up as the model though David himself sinned gravely, so that integrity of heart here means wholehearted loyalty to the LORD with repentance, not sinless perfection, and that such obedience is the fruit of grace.

Both traditions read the call to obedience as real and serious.

verses.text: then I will establish the throne of your kingdom over Israel forever, as I promised to David your father, saying, ‘There shall not fail from you a man on the throne of Israel.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Then God will establish Solomon’s throne over Israel forever, as he promised David that a man would not fail from him on Israel’s throne. The promise echoes earlier words (2:4; 8:25).

Arminian readers note that the promise is offered to Solomon as an invitation, and that the blessing of a secure throne is linked to the king’s faithful response.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that this promise stands within the larger covenant with David, in which God promised discipline for sin but not removal of his steadfast love (2 Samuel 7:14–15), and that Christians in both traditions see that promise fulfilled ultimately in Christ.

Both traditions read the Davidic covenant here as shared ground, consistent with the site’s treatment of 2 Samuel 7.

verses.text: But if you turn away from following me, you or your children, and not keep my commandments and my statutes which I have set before you, but go and serve other gods and worship them,
verses.arminianNotes:
But if Solomon or his children turn away, fail to keep God’s commands, and go and serve other gods, consequences will follow. The warning centers on idolatry.

Arminian readers note that the warning is real and addressed to people who could actually turn away, showing that covenant privilege does not remove the responsibility of continued faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that warnings like this are among the means God uses to keep his people faithful, and that the site’s existing box at 1 Samuel 12:22 already addresses how the two traditions relate such warnings to perseverance.

Both traditions agree that serving other gods is the gravest covenant breach, and both see this warning fulfilled tragically in Israel’s later history.

verses.text: then I will cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and I will cast this house, which I have made holy for my name, out of my sight; and Israel will be a proverb and a byword among all peoples.
verses.arminianNotes:
God says he will then cut Israel off from the land, cast the house from his sight, and Israel will become a proverb and a byword among all peoples. The language echoes Deuteronomy 28:37.

Arminian readers note that the holiness of the house does not protect a disobedient people; God’s presence is not a guarantee that can be presumed upon apart from covenant faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s judgment on his own house shows that he is not bound to a building, and that this warning was fulfilled in the destruction of the temple and the exile (2 Kings 25:9–11), while his promise to David still pointed beyond that judgment.

Both traditions read the warning as shared ground: covenant unfaithfulness brings real judgment.

verses.text: Though this house is so high, yet everyone who passes by it will be astonished and hiss; and they will say, ‘Why has the LORD done this to this land and to this house?’
verses.arminianNotes:
Though the house is so high, everyone who passes by will be astonished and hiss, asking why the LORD has done this to the land and the house. The nations will notice.

Arminian readers note that the very grandeur of the temple will make its ruin more striking, and that God’s judgment on his people is meant to teach the watching world as well as Israel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the question echoes Deuteronomy 29:24–26, showing that the warnings given through Moses still stand, and that God’s dealings with his people are a public testimony to his holiness among the nations.

Both traditions agree that God’s honor among the nations is at stake in how his people live.

verses.text: and they will answer, ‘Because they abandoned the LORD their God, who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt, and embraced other gods, and worshiped them, and served them. Therefore the LORD has brought all this evil on them.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The answer will be that they abandoned the LORD who brought their fathers out of Egypt, embraced other gods and served them, so the LORD brought this evil on them. The cause is stated plainly.

Arminian readers note that the judgment is explained as the result of the people’s own choice to abandon God, which shows that God’s justice responds to real human unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the reference to the exodus grounds Israel’s obligation in God’s prior saving grace, so that idolatry is ingratitude toward the God who redeemed them, and that his judgment is just.

Both traditions treat this verse as shared ground: God’s past grace calls for faithfulness, and abandoning him brings judgment.
